e.etymology: Usually explained as a Chewa name from Malawi, from the verb seka (to laugh). In the US it rose after Sekani Carter, the little brother in the novel The Hate U Give (2017) and its 2018 film.
namesakes: Sekani Carter (little brother in The Hate U Give)

e.etymology: A short form of Ashley, Asher and Ashton, and a surname in its own right, from Old English aesc (ash tree).

assoc.t: Ash Ketchum, the trainer hero of Pokemon
Ash Williams, hero of the Evil Dead films

e.note: Also the everyday word for what a fire leaves behind.

e.etymology: A modern Hebrew name from rom (height, elevation) with the ending for my. The same sound is the German pet name Romy, short for Rosemarie.
A spelling of Emmeline, the medieval English form of Old French Ameline, from the Germanic element amal (work). It is not derived from Emma, though it is often heard as Emma plus -line.
The Italian form of Clara, from Latin clarus (bright, clear, famous). Saint Clare of Assisi, the follower of Saint Francis, is Santa Chiara in Italian.
e.note: Americans often misread it as chee-AR-uh; the Italian sound is kee-AH-rah.

e.etymology: Feminine of Antonius, a Roman family name of unknown, possibly Etruscan, origin; the popular gloss priceless is a later guess. It is the name of the heroine of Willa Cather's 1918 novel My Antonia.
namesakes: Antonia Shimerda (heroine of Willa Cather's My Antonia)

e.etymology: A short form of Rachel, Hebrew for ewe, and a feminine spelling of Ray. Rae is also a Scottish surname. Today it is used most often as a middle name.
namesakes: Issa Rae (creator and star of Insecure)
Addison Rae (TikTok star and pop singer)

e.etymology: Probably a variant of Xenia, from Greek xenia (hospitality), from xenos (stranger, guest). Its use as a baby name dates from the TV series Xena: Warrior Princess, which ran from 1995 to 2001.

assoc.t: Xena: Warrior Princess, 1990s TV action heroine

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that joins Ray or Rae to the -lee ending of Kaylee and Baylee.
A variant of Caroline with the -lyn ending, used since the 19th century. Caroline is a feminine form of Charles, from a Germanic word for a free man.
namesakes: Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy (wife of John F. Kennedy Jr.)
Carolyn Keene (pen name on the Nancy Drew mysteries)
Carolyn Jones (Morticia in the 1960s Addams Family series)

e.etymology: The English name of the fragrant purple-flowered herb and of its color, from Old French lavandre and medieval Latin lavandula. It is also an old surname for a launderer.
namesakes: Lavender Brown (Gryffindor student in Harry Potter)

e.etymology: A spelling of Natalie or Nathalie favored in Hispanic families. Natalie comes from Latin natale domini, the birth of the Lord, a name for Christmas.

The Greek and Latin form of Josiah, a Hebrew name usually read as the Lord supports; it is the spelling used in the King James New Testament. It is also the everyday form of the name in Spanish and Portuguese.
From the Irish surname O Bradain, descendant of Bradan, a personal name meaning salmon. It can also come from an English place name read as broad valley. It caught on as a first name in the 1990s.
From the purple quartz gemstone, the birthstone for February. Its name is Greek amethystos (not drunk), because the stone was believed to ward off intoxication.

assoc.t: amethyst, the purple gem and February birthstone
Amethyst, a Crystal Gem in the cartoon Steven Universe

e.meaning: pet form of Mary; also read as Mary plus Ann
e.etymology: A variant of Marion, a medieval French pet form of Marie (Mary), later also understood as Mary plus Ann. In Poland, Romania and Germany Marian is a man's name from Latin Marianus.
namesakes: Maid Marian (Robin Hood's love)
Marian Anderson (contralto who sang at the Lincoln Memorial in 1939)
Marian Paroo (the librarian in The Music Man)

assoc.t: Marian, the adjective for things of the Virgin Mary

e.etymology: A K spelling of Christopher, from Greek Christophoros (bearer of Christ), the name behind the legend of Saint Christopher carrying the Christ child across a river.

e.meaning: one who warns; also observer, overseer
e.etymology: An English spelling of more than one Arabic name: Nadhir (warner), a Quranic title of the Prophet Muhammad that is said Nazir in Urdu and Persian, and Nazir (observer, overseer).

e.meaning: the country India, named for the Indus River
e.etymology: From the name of the country, which goes back through Greek and Persian to Sanskrit sindhu (river), the Indus. English families used it during British rule in India, and Gone with the Wind has an India Wilkes.
namesakes: India Arie (Grammy-winning R&B singer)
India Wilkes (Gone with the Wind character)
e.note: Everyone will think of the country first; some see the name as a leftover of British colonial fashion.

e.etymology: The French spelling of Natalie, from Late Latin Natalia, from natalis dies, the birthday of Christ. The h is silent.
namesakes: Nathalie Emmanuel (Game of Thrones and Fast and Furious actress)

e.etymology: An older spelling of Molly, a medieval English pet form of Mary in which the r became l, as it did in Sally from Sarah. Mollie was the more common spelling in 19th-century America.

assoc.t: molly, street name for the drug MDMA (sounds the same)

e.etymology: A 20th-century American coinage from Jay plus the -lene ending of Charlene and Jolene.

e.meaning: short for Jordan, the river whose name means to flow down
e.etymology: A pet form of Jordan, from the river whose Hebrew name means to descend or flow down. In Dutch use Jordy is a spelling of Jordi, the Catalan form of George.
namesakes: Jordy Nelson (Green Bay Packers wide receiver)

e.meaning: name of a biblical mountain; often read as seen by the Lord
e.etymology: From Mount Moriah, where Genesis sets the binding of Isaac and where Solomon later built the Temple. The Hebrew meaning is uncertain; a traditional reading ties it to God seeing or providing.

assoc.t: Mount Moriah, biblical site of the binding of Isaac

e.meaning: waited for (Hawaiian); also a native Hawaiian tree
e.etymology: In Hawaiian, kalia means waited for and is also the name of a native tree. Many American families use it simply as a spelling in the Kaliyah and Kalea family.
A pet form of Bob, the rhyming nickname of Rob, short for Robert, a Germanic name from hrod (fame) and berht (bright). Bobby has long been given as a full name in the United States.
namesakes: Bobby Kennedy (Robert F. Kennedy, attorney general and senator)
Bobby Fischer (chess world champion)
Bobby Flay (celebrity chef)

assoc.t: bobby pin, the small hair clip
bobby, British slang for a police officer

e.etymology: A contracted form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath. In the US it is used mainly in Hispanic families, alongside Lisbeth and Lizeth.
From an English surname meaning son of Brand, a medieval name from Old Norse brandr (sword, firebrand). In some families it comes instead from the place name Branston.

assoc.t: Richard Branson, founder of the Virgin Group

e.etymology: From Hebrew menachem (one who comforts), the name of a king of Israel in the Bible. It is traditional in Jewish families, and in Chabad it honors Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson, the Lubavitcher Rebbe.
namesakes: Menachem Begin (Israeli prime minister and Nobel Peace laureate)
Menachem Mendel Schneerson (the Lubavitcher Rebbe)

e.etymology: From an English surname first given to Bretons, the people of Brittany in France, many of whom settled in England after the Norman Conquest.
namesakes: Brett Favre (Hall of Fame quarterback)
Brett Kavanaugh (Supreme Court justice)

e.etymology: From Arabic jamal (beauty), the noun from the verb to be beautiful. It has been one of the best-known Arabic names in African American families since the 1970s.
namesakes: Jamal Murray (NBA guard)
Jamal Khashoggi (Saudi journalist killed in 2018)
Jamal Malik (hero of Slumdog Millionaire)

e.etymology: The German and Scandinavian spelling of Jacob, from Hebrew Ya'aqov. Genesis ties the name to the heel Jacob grasped at birth; another reading is may God protect.
namesakes: Jakob Dylan (Wallflowers singer, son of Bob Dylan)
